analysis.one_liner: Limits secret court surveillance orders and requires people eventually be told their data was taken.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2026 with a bipartisan group of four senators, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no hearing, vote, or further action has occurred.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how federal and state courts handle secret surveillance orders — wiretaps, search warrants, records demands to phone and internet companies, and tracking devices. It would cap initial secrecy periods at 180 days, require courts to justify each extension with specific facts, publish public docket records showing how many surveillance orders judges grant and deny, and require the government to notify people that their communications or records were taken once secrecy is no longer justified. It also authorizes about $26 million to help courts, including state and tribal courts, build the required systems.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose phone records, emails, cloud files, or location data are secretly taken by the government. Today many people are never told — the government can delay or prevent notice for years through repeated secret extensions. The bill guarantees that notice eventually reaches the target, caps how long courts can keep the paperwork sealed, lets members of the public ask a judge to unseal orders, and creates annual public reports on how often prosecutors get secret surveillance and secrecy orders. It also protects law-abiding people swept into dragnet requests aimed at others.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the initial sealing of a surveillance order, its application, and the inventory of what was taken at 180 days after execution or the end of surveillance; extensions require renewed justifications, and a second or later extension requires a particularized, fact-specific showing that secrecy is still needed and that redactions would not suffice [S2].

Requires the government to serve people with a copy of the warrant or order used against them once delay is no longer justified, and to notify subscribers within 7 days when it receives data through voluntary provider disclosures, with delays allowed only under the reformed section 2705 process [S2].

Prohibits indefinite sealing by requiring automatic unsealing the next business day after a seal expires, and creates a public docket record for every surveillance case showing the type of order, the agency, the disposition, and the seal expiration date [S2].

Requires judges and the Administrative Office of the Courts to publish annual public reports on surveillance orders, pen registers, trap-and-trace devices, and preclusion-of-notice orders, including how many were granted, modified, or denied [S2].
Requires inventories to disclose whether the government took or searched more than the court authorized, so overshoots by law enforcement are documented and returned to the court [S2].

Authorizes $1 million to the federal court system and up to $25 million in grants to state and tribal courts to build the electronic docketing and filing systems the bill requires, with delayed deadlines for courts that lack them [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies and federal prosecutors lose the ability to keep surveillance orders sealed indefinitely and to delay notice to targets without meeting stricter standards. Courts bear the cost and work of docketing, publishing, and reporting on surveillance cases, though the bill appropriates federal money to cover it. Communications providers face new duties, such as copies of subpoenas being docketed and cooperation with inventories, in exchange for limits on indefinite gag orders.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement, prosecutors, and court systems

drawbacks.text: Public docket records and published reports could still reveal sensitive details about investigations; even generic case captions and category-level reporting may tip off targets or expose investigative patterns, which is the core concern law enforcement raises against sealing limits [S2].

The administrative burden on courts is substantial: electronic filing, public bulk-downloadable dockets, annual judge-by-judge reports, and automatic unsealing machinery all need to be built, and state and tribal courts without electronic docketing get four years plus renewable one-year security-delay extensions before complying [S2].
The main provisions take effect two years after enactment, so the secrecy practices the bill targets would continue unchanged for at least two years even if it passed immediately [S2].

The 180-day cap on delayed notice for subpoenas and emergency requests still allows multiple consecutive extensions, meaning secrecy can stretch well past six months when a judge agrees to renew it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and structural: a legal right to eventually learn that the government took your records, and public statistics on how often secret surveillance happens — something currently known only to prosecutors and judges. The costs are mostly administrative and are funded by the bill itself. The strongest honest objection is that transparency and secrecy exist in tension, and the bill resolves it by allowing real secrecy for up to 180 days at a time with escalating justification for extensions, which is a genuine middle ground rather than an abdication. The design is careful — it keeps sealed handling for endangerment, flight, tampering, and intimidation cases — so the trade-off weighs clearly in favor of the notice and transparency provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on February 25, 2026, and the committee has taken no further action on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Government Surveillance Transparency Act of 2026 on February 25, 2026, joined by Sens. Mike Daines, Mike Lee, and Cory Booker — two Republicans and two Democrats [S1][S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action appears in the action history [S4].

Because the 119th Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027, the bill is still technically alive, but with no committee action on record it currently sits in the stage where most bills stop [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet, because the bill has not advanced or been voted down. For now, the existing system — where surveillance orders can be kept sealed and notice to targets delayed indefinitely — continues unchanged, which is the outcome prosecutors and agencies prefer and the outcome civil liberties groups want changed. The beneficiaries of the current state of affairs are law enforcement agencies that operate under today's secrecy rules.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 25, 2026, to require eventual notice of surveillance to targets, cap sealing periods, and create public reporting of surveillance orders.

for.name: Sens. Mike Daines and Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: Democratic cosponsor, Senate Judiciary Committee member

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 25, 2026; no hearing, markup, or vote on it appears in the record since.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four Senate sponsors split evenly between the parties (two Democrats, two Republicans), but with no votes or committee action yet, the partisan shape of opposition — if any — is not visible in the record.

industries.industry: Federal and state law enforcement and prosecutors
industries.note: The bill takes away their ability to keep surveillance orders sealed indefinitely and to delay or preclude notice to targets without escalating judicial justification. Agencies would also have to file annual reports exposing how often they obtain secret surveillance and secrecy orders.

industries.industry: Communications and cloud service providers (phone, internet, email, and data storage companies)
industries.note: Providers face new compliance duties — subpoena copies must be docketed, and inventories must document what they disclosed. In exchange, the bill ends the risk of open-ended gag orders by capping nondisclosure at defined, renewable 180-day periods, which many providers have publicly sought.

industries.industry: State, tribal, and federal court systems
industries.note: Courts must build electronic filing, public docketing, and annual reporting systems. The bill funds this with $1 million for federal courts and up to $25 million in grants to state and tribal courts, and gives courts without electronic systems extra years to comply.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no scheduled hearing or markup, which is where the large majority of Senate bills stop. Its bipartisan sponsorship and lack of an industry opponent give it a plausible path if the committee takes it up, but absent committee action its realistic routes are a standalone markup that has not been scheduled or attachment as language to a broader, must-pass bill such as a Justice Department reauthorization. With roughly ten months left in the session, the most likely outcome remains no action.
